blocks.text:
Open Instagram and the first thing you see is a feed: a scrolling column of photos and videos from people you follow, sorted so the most relevant, most recent content sits at the top. That single screen is deceptively hard to build well at scale, because it sits at the intersection of two very different engineering problems bolted together. The first is a media pipeline problem: accepting a photo or video upload, storing it durably, generating the thumbnails and compressed renditions a mobile app actually needs, and serving all of that back through a CDN fast enough that scrolling feels instant. The second is a fan-out problem: the moment you post, that content somehow has to reach every one of your followers' feeds, and if you happen to have fifty million followers, "somehow" needs a genuinely different answer than it does for an account with two hundred.

Neither half of this problem is optional, and neither is trivial on its own. We are going to design the core of a photo and video sharing platform: users upload media, follow each other, and see a feed of posts from the people they follow, with likes and comments layered on top.

blocks.text: Consider a platform with 200 million daily active users, each opening the app and refreshing their feed roughly 5 times a day, and 20 million posts created daily. Feed reads work out to 200,000,000 times 5, which is 1 billion feed reads a day, or roughly 1,000,000,000 divided by 86,400, about 11,600 reads per second on average. Post creation, at 20 million a day, averages around 20,000,000 divided by 86,400, roughly 230 writes per second. The ratio between those two numbers, about 50 to 1, is the single number that shapes almost every architectural decision that follows.

blocks.text: Here is where the celebrity problem becomes concrete with real numbers. An average user with 300 followers posting once generates 300 feed-cache writes, trivial. A celebrity account with 50 million followers posting once would naively generate 50 million feed-cache writes for that single post, an amount of work that would visibly strain the system, all triggered by one tap of a button. That single worked example is the entire justification for the hybrid fan-out strategy covered in section 7.

blocks.text: Uploads and reads travel through almost entirely separate paths in this system. A client uploads media directly to blob storage using a short-lived, pre-signed URL, so raw photo and video bytes never pass through the application servers at all; once the upload finishes, the client confirms with the API, which kicks off asynchronous processing and fan-out. Reads, by contrast, almost never touch blob storage or the processing pipeline directly, instead hitting a precomputed feed cache.

blocks.title: Why upload directly to blob storage
blocks.text: Routing every photo and video byte through the application servers would turn upload traffic into a bandwidth and compute bottleneck for no real benefit. A pre-signed URL lets the client talk to blob storage directly, with the application server only involved in issuing that short-lived, scoped credential and later confirming the upload finished, keeping the actual heavy data transfer entirely off the request-serving fleet.

blocks.alt: An entity relationship diagram showing users authoring posts and following each other, with posts receiving likes

blocks.text: The Post table holds metadata, not media bytes, mirroring the same split seen in other read-heavy content systems. An index on authorId plus createdAt supports both profile-grid views and, for celebrity accounts, the read-time merge described earlier. The Follow table is queried in both directions: "who does this user follow" for fan out, and "who follows this user" less often but still needed for follower-count display.

blocks.text: The feed cache itself deserves a specific data-modeling call-out. For each user, it stores an ordered list, typically implemented as a sorted set keyed by post timestamp, of the post ids that belong in their feed. This is deliberately a thin index of ids, not a copy of the full post content, so a single new post being fanned out to a million followers means writing a million small, cheap entries, not a million copies of the actual post data.

A worked example sequence diagram: Alice posts a photo, it gets fanned out to her followers' feed caches, and Bob, one of her followers, opens the app moments later and already sees it

blocks.text: Alice, an account with a modest 400 followers, posts a photo of her lunch. The upload service confirms the media landed in blob storage, kicks off thumbnail generation, and immediately triggers fan out: since 400 is nowhere near the celebrity threshold, the fan out service pushes her new post id directly into all 400 of her followers' feed caches. Moments later, Bob, one of those followers, opens the app; his feed read hits his already-updated cache and Alice's post appears right at the top, with no extra work needed at read time.

blocks.text: Now picture the same sequence for a celebrity account with 50 million followers. Proactively pushing to 50 million feed caches synchronously (or even asynchronously, in one giant burst) would be an enormous, wasteful spike of write load, most of which serves followers who will not open the app again for hours. Instead, that post is simply written once to the celebrity's own posts table, and each follower's feed read merges it in on the fly, at read time, spreading that cost across millions of separate, cheap read requests instead of one massive write storm.

blocks.text: The feed cache, described throughout this doc, is the centerpiece of the entire read path: every normal feed read is, ideally, a single cache lookup and nothing more. Like and comment counts get their own lighter-weight caching and aggregation story.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing like taps landing in an in-memory increment buffer, flushed periodically by an aggregation worker into the post metadata database as an approximate count

blocks.text: Rather than issuing a database write on every single like tap, which would create enormous write contention on a viral post's single counter row, likes accumulate briefly in a fast in-memory buffer and get flushed to the database in small batches every few seconds. The displayed like count is therefore approximate and slightly delayed, which is an entirely acceptable trade for a number nobody is relying on to be perfectly precise in real time.

blocks.text: Two asynchronous pipelines run off queues here: media processing, which takes a raw upload and produces the various thumbnail and compressed renditions the mobile app actually requests, and fan out, which takes a confirmed post and pushes it into follower feed caches. Both are decoupled from the user-facing upload request specifically so a slow processing job never makes the uploader sit and wait; the post appears as "processing" almost immediately and becomes fully visible once the async work finishes, typically within a few seconds.

blocks.alt: A load balancer distributing requests across stateless API instances

blocks.text: Every API-facing service here is stateless, so straightforward round robin or least-connections load balancing works fine, with no sticky session requirement, since nothing about a client's session lives on any one particular instance.

blocks.alt: A flowchart showing fan out workers being added when the fan out queue depth grows

blocks.text: The feed and upload services scale horizontally with request volume in the usual way. The fan out workers scale specifically off queue depth rather than request rate, since their workload is bursty and driven by how many posts are actively being fanned out at any given moment, which does not track cleanly with raw API request volume.

blocks.text: Post metadata and the follow graph both shard by user id, as shown earlier. The feed cache, being a Redis-style in-memory store, shards the same way, with each user's feed entirely owned by one shard, which keeps a feed read a single, targeted lookup rather than a fan-out query across the whole cache cluster.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing the choice of availability plus eventual consistency, justified by the fact that a feed a few seconds stale or a like count slightly off is harmless

blocks.text: Almost everything in this system leans toward availability and eventual consistency over strict correctness. A feed that is a few seconds behind the absolute latest post, or a like count that is briefly a little low because a batch has not flushed yet, causes no real harm to anyone and is invisible to the vast majority of users. The one place worth being more careful is the follow graph itself: a user unfollowing someone and then still briefly seeing their posts is a mild annoyance, but the system tolerates it as an acceptable, short-lived inconsistency rather than paying for synchronous, strongly consistent updates everywhere.

blocks.alt: A primary feed cache node with a replica node, failing over if the primary goes down

blocks.text: The feed cache runs with replicas so a single node failure does not wipe out a slice of users' feeds entirely, just briefly increases read latency during failover. If the fan out queue backs up or a worker crashes mid-job, the job simply gets retried, since fan out writes are idempotent (writing the same post id into a feed cache twice has no different effect than writing it once).

blocks.text: Pre-signed upload URLs are scoped narrowly (a specific bucket path, a short expiration window, a maximum file size) so they cannot be abused to upload arbitrary content elsewhere. Private accounts need their follow-graph and feed logic to actually enforce visibility, not just hide content in the client UI, since a determined user could otherwise query the API directly and bypass a client-side-only privacy check. Standard authentication and rate limiting protect the upload and follow endpoints from abuse.

blocks.text: The two most important operational signals here are fan out queue depth and lag (a growing backlog means users are not seeing new posts from their followed accounts promptly) and feed cache hit rate (a drop usually means either a cache eviction storm or a fan out pipeline that has fallen behind). Media processing job failure rate and latency round out the picture, since a stuck processing pipeline leaves posts visibly "still processing" for users.

blocks.alt: A map of two bottlenecks: a celebrity post triggering a massive naive fan out, fixed by the hybrid strategy skipping proactive push for celebrity accounts, and a viral post overwhelming blob storage reads, fixed by CDN absorption

blocks.text: The celebrity fan-out problem is the headline architectural challenge in this entire system, and the hybrid push and pull strategy exists specifically to defuse it. The second pressure point, a single photo suddenly going viral and being fetched an enormous number of times, is handled the same way most read-heavy media systems handle it: lean on the CDN to absorb nearly all of that traffic before it ever reaches origin blob storage.

blocks.alt: A comparison of fan out on write, cheap reads but expensive celebrity writes, versus fan out on read, cheap writes but an expensive merge on every read

blocks.text: Fan out on write makes every feed read trivially cheap (just look up the precomputed list), at the cost of a write amplifying into potentially millions of feed-cache writes for a popular account. Fan out on read makes every write cheap (write the post once), at the cost of every single feed read needing to merge content from every followed account live, which does not scale as follower counts and following counts both grow. The hybrid approach used throughout this design takes the cheap-read benefit of fan-out-on-write for the 99.9 percent of accounts that are not celebrities, and falls back to fan-out-on-read merging specifically for the rare celebrity accounts where proactive fan out would be prohibitively expensive.

blocks.alt: A cost breakdown dominated by media storage, with variable CDN bandwidth cost scaling with views

blocks.text: Media storage is the largest and steadily growing cost, since photos and videos accumulate and are rarely deleted. Storing older, rarely-viewed media on a cheaper storage tier after an inactivity window, while keeping recent and actively-viewed content on faster storage, is the most effective lever here without touching the user experience at all.
